question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=e^{x + y + z}$, where $x=s + 2 t$, $y=- s + t$, $z=- s^{2}$. Calculate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}$ in terms of $s$ and $t$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

Hold $t$ fixed. Multiply along the three paths and add:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial s}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=e^{x + y + z} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=e^{x + y + z} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=e^{x + y + z}\end{aligned}
$$

Write these partials in terms of $s$ and $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=e^{- s^{2} + 3 t} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=e^{- s^{2} + 3 t} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=e^{- s^{2} + 3 t}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each intermediate variable with respect to $s$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}&=1 \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}&=-1 \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial s}&=- 2 s\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the matching factors, then collect terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}&=\left(e^{- s^{2} + 3 t}\right)\left(1\right) \\ &{}+\left(e^{- s^{2} + 3 t}\right)\left(-1\right) \\ &{}+\left(e^{- s^{2} + 3 t}\right)\left(- 2 s\right) \\ &=- 2 s e^{- s^{2} + 3 t}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=e^{x + y + z}$, where $x=- 2 s + 2 t$, $y=- 2 t^{2}$, $z=s - t$. Calculate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}$ in terms of $s$ and $t$.
question.:question/worked-solution:

Hold $s$ fixed. Multiply along the three paths and add:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial t}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=e^{x + y + z} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=e^{x + y + z} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=e^{x + y + z}\end{aligned}
$$

Write these partials in terms of $s$ and $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=e^{- s - 2 t^{2} + t} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=e^{- s - 2 t^{2} + t} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=e^{- s - 2 t^{2} + t}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each intermediate variable with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}&=2 \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}&=- 4 t \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial t}&=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the matching factors, then collect terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}&=\left(e^{- s - 2 t^{2} + t}\right)\left(2\right) \\ &{}+\left(e^{- s - 2 t^{2} + t}\right)\left(- 4 t\right) \\ &{}+\left(e^{- s - 2 t^{2} + t}\right)\left(-1\right) \\ &=- \left(4 t - 1\right) e^{- s - 2 t^{2} + t}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=x y z$, where $x=s e^{- 3 t}$, $y=-2$, $z=t e^{- 2 s}$. Calculate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}$ in terms of $s$ and $t$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

Hold $t$ fixed. Multiply along the three paths and add:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial s}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=y z \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=x z \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=x y\end{aligned}
$$

Write these partials in terms of $s$ and $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=- 2 t e^{- 2 s} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=s t e^{- 2 s - 3 t} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=- 2 s e^{- 3 t}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each intermediate variable with respect to $s$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}&=e^{- 3 t} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}&=0 \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial s}&=- 2 t e^{- 2 s}\end{aligned}
$$

Combine exponential factors using $e^A e^B=e^{A+B}$ when collecting the path products. Substitute the matching factors, then collect terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}&=\left(- 2 t e^{- 2 s}\right)\left(e^{- 3 t}\right) \\ &{}+\left(s t e^{- 2 s - 3 t}\right)\left(0\right) \\ &{}+\left(- 2 s e^{- 3 t}\right)\left(- 2 t e^{- 2 s}\right) \\ &=2 t \left(2 s - 1\right) e^{- 2 s - 3 t}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the scalar line integral

$$
\int_C (x^2+y)\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$

where $C$ is given by $y=2x+1$ for $0\le x\le 1$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $x=t$ and substitute the line equation:

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,2t+1\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$

Then

$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle 1,2\rangle,\qquad \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5.
$$

Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=t^2+(2t+1)=t^2+2t+1.
$$

Multiply by the speed and integrate each term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C (x^2+y)\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\sqrt5\int_0^1(t^2+2t+1)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\sqrt5\left[\frac{t^3}{3}+t^2+t\right]_0^1\\
&=\sqrt5\left(\frac13+1+1\right)\\
&=\frac{7\sqrt5}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the scalar line integral

$$
\int_C x\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$

where $C$ is given by $y=2x$ for $0\le x\le 1$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $x=t$. The explicit equation gives

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,2t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$

Differentiate the curve and compute its speed:

$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle 1,2\rangle,\qquad \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{1^2+2^2}=\sqrt5.
$$

The scalar function is $f(x,y)=x$, so $f(\mathbf r(t))=t$. Include the speed factor when replacing $\mathrm{d}s$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C x\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\sqrt5\int_0^1 t\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\sqrt5\left[\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^1\\
&=\frac{\sqrt5}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

\int_C 2y^2\,\mathrm{d}s,

question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the explicit curve to set

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,e^t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le\ln2.
$$

The speed is now variable:

$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle1,e^t\rangle,\qquad \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{1+e^{2t}}.
$$

Since $f(\mathbf r(t))=2e^{2t}$, the line integral becomes

$$
\int_C 2y^2\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^{\ln2}2e^{2t}\sqrt{1+e^{2t}}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Choose $u=1+e^{2t}$, so $\mathrm{d}u=2e^{2t}\,\mathrm{d}t$. The bounds change from $t=0$ and $t=\ln2$ to $u=2$ and $u=5$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C 2y^2\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\int_2^5 u^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}u\\
&=\left[\frac23u^{3/2}\right]_2^5\\
&=\frac23(5\sqrt5-2\sqrt2)\\
&=\frac{10\sqrt5-4\sqrt2}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the portion of $y=\ln(1+x^2)$ with $x>0$ between its intersections with the horizontal lines $y=\ln 2$ and $y=\ln 5$.

Which definite integral is equivalent to

$$
\int_C \left(xe^y-y\right)\,\mathrm{d}s
$$

using $x=t$? Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the horizontal lines to find the endpoints. Since $x>0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln(1+x^2)=\ln 2&\implies 1+x^2=2\implies x=1,\\
\ln(1+x^2)=\ln 5&\implies 1+x^2=5\implies x=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The positive branch is increasing, so these intersections bound one section. Parametrize it by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,\ln(1+t^2)\rangle,\qquad 1\le t\le 2.
$$

Apply the chain rule before forming the arc-length factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\left\langle 1,\frac{2t}{1+t^2}\right\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{2t}{1+t^2}\right)^2}
=\sqrt{1+\frac{4t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute both coordinates into $f(x,y)=xe^y-y$. Using $e^{\ln(1+t^2)}=1+t^2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf r(t))
&=t e^{\ln(1+t^2)}-\ln(1+t^2)\\
&=t(1+t^2)-\ln(1+t^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, multiply the scalar by the speed and use the $t=x$ bounds:

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s
=\int_1^2 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Substituting gives the required definite integral:

$$
\int_1^2 \left[t(1+t^2)-\ln(1+t^2)\right]\sqrt{1+\frac{4t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

This substitutes $xy$ but omits the arc-length factor.
The $x$-bounds are $0$ and $1$, the scalar is $t e^t$, and the speed is $\sqrt{1+e^{2t}}$.
For $t=x$, solve $e^x=1$ and $e^x=e$; the limits are $0$ and $1$.

question.:question/worked-solution:
The rows follow the order in $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)$: $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$, $\mathbf c$. The scalar triple product equals the determinant of these rows.

$$
\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)=\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row using the cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=0\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=0-2(1\cdot3-2\cdot2)+(1\cdot1-0\cdot2) \\ &=0+2+1 \\ &=3.\end{aligned}
$$

The rows follow the order in $\mathbf r\cdot(\mathbf q\times\mathbf p)$: $\mathbf r$, $\mathbf q$, $\mathbf p$. The scalar triple product equals the determinant of these rows.

$$
\mathbf r\cdot(\mathbf q\times\mathbf p)=\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row using the cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}+(-1)\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ &=2(1\cdot2-3(-2)) \\ &\quad -3((-2)\cdot2-3\cdot1) \\ &\quad +(-1)((-2)(-2)-1\cdot1) \\ &=16+21-3 \\ &=34.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose

\qquad \mathbf{a}=\langle1,2,-1\rangle.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the supplied cross product; no individual coordinates for $\mathbf{b}$ or $\mathbf{c}$ are needed. First take its dot product with $\mathbf{a}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a}\cdot\bigl((2\mathbf{b})\times(-\mathbf{c})\bigr)
&=\langle1,2,-1\rangle\cdot\langle4,-6,2\rangle\\
&=1(4)+2(-6)+(-1)(2)\\
&=-10.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $T=\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})$. Factoring out the two scalars gives

$$
-2T=-10,\qquad T=5.
$$

Swapping $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ changes the sign:

$$
\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c})=-T=-5.
$$

Now factor the scalars out of the requested product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2\mathbf{b})\cdot\bigl((3\mathbf{a})\times(-\mathbf{c})\bigr)
&=2(3)(-1)\bigl[\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c})\bigr]\\
&=(-6)(-5)\\
&=30.
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, swap $\mathbf{a}$ and $2\mathbf{b}$ in the computed product $-10$, then multiply the new outer vector $\mathbf{a}$ by $3$: $-3(-10)=30$.

\begin{aligned}D&=0\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\ &=0(2\cdot 2-0\cdot 3) \\ &\quad -3(2\cdot 2-0\cdot (-2)) \\ &\quad +2(2\cdot 3-2\cdot (-2)) \\ &=0(4)-3(4)+2(10) \\ &=0-12+20 \\ &=8.\end{aligned}
